passage_1.text:
I have elaborated a framework for analyzing the contradictory pulls on Indian nationalist ideology in its struggle against the dominance of colonialism and the resolution it offered to those contradictions. Briefly, this resolution was built around a separation of the domain of culture into two spheres, the material and the spiritual. It was in the material sphere that the claims of Western civilization were the most powerful. Science, technology, rational forms of economic organization, modern methods of statecraft, these had given the European countries the strength to subjugate the non-European people. To overcome this domination, the colonized people had to learn those superior techniques of organizing material life and incorporate them within their own cultures. But this could not mean the imitation of the West in every aspect of life, for then the very distinction between the West and the East would vanish the self-identity of national culture would itself be threatened.

The discourse of nationalism shows that the material/spiritual distinction was condensed into an analogous, but ideologically far more powerful, dichotomy: that between the outer and the inner. Applying the inner/outer distinction to the matter of concrete day-to-day living separates the social space into ghar and bāhir, the home and the world. The world is the external, the domain of the material; the home represents one's inner spiritual self, one's true identity. The world is a treacherous terrain of the pursuit of material interests, where practical considerations reign supreme. It is also typically the domain of the male. The home in its essence must remain unaffected by the profane activities of the material world—and woman is its representation. And so one gets an identification of social roles by gender to correspond with the separation of the social space into ghar and bāhir.

The colonial situation, and the ideological response of nationalism to the critique of Indian tradition, introduced an entirely new substance to these dichotomies and effected their transformation. The material/spiritual dichotomy, to which the terms world and home corresponded, had acquired a very special significance in the nationalist mind. The world was where the European power had challenged the non-European peoples and, by virtue of its superior material culture, had subjugated them. But, the nationalists asserted, it had failed to colonize the inner, essential, identity of the East which lay in its distinctive, and superior, spiritual culture. In the entire phase of the national struggle, the crucial need was to protect, preserve and strengthen the inner core of the national culture, its spiritual essence.

Once we match this new meaning of the home/world dichotomy with the identification of social roles by gender, we get the ideological framework within which nationalism answered the women's question. It would be a grave error to see in this, as liberals are apt to in their despair at the many marks of social conservatism in nationalist practice, a total rejection of the West. Quite the contrary: the nationalist paradigm in fact supplied an ideological principle of selection.

passage_2.text:
It has been said that knowledge, or the problem of knowledge, is the scandal of philosophy. The scandal is philosophy's apparent inability to show how, when and why we can be sure that we know something or, indeed, that we know anything. Philosopher Michael Williams writes: 'Is it possible to obtain knowledge at all? This problem is pressing because there are powerful arguments, some very ancient, for the conclusion that it is not. Scepticism is the skeleton in Western rationalism's closet'. While it is not clear that the scandal matters to anyone but philosophers, philosophers point out that it should matter to everyone, at least given a certain conception of knowledge. For, they explain, unless we can ground our claims to knowledge as such, which is to say, distinguish it from mere opinion, superstition, fantasy, wishful thinking, ideology, illusion or delusion, then the actions we take on the basis of presumed knowledge - boarding an airplane, swallowing a pill, finding someone guilty of a crime - will be irrational and unjustifiable.

That is all quite serious-sounding but so also are the rattlings of the skeleton: that is, the sceptic's contention that we cannot be sure that we know anything at least not if we think of knowledge as something like having a correct mental representation of reality, and not if we think of reality as something like things as they are in themselves, independent of our perceptions, ideas or descriptions. For, the sceptic will note, since reality, under that conception of it, is outside our ken (we cannot catch a glimpse of things in themselves around the corner of our own eyes; we cannot form an idea of reality that floats above the processes of our conceiving it), we have no way to compare our mental representations with things as they are in themselves and therefore no way to determine whether they are correct or incorrect. Thus the sceptic may repeat (rattling loudly), you cannot be sure you 'know' something or anything at all – at least not, he may add (rattling softly before disappearing), if that is the way you conceive 'knowledge'.

There are a number of ways to handle this situation. The most common is to ignore it. Most people outside the academy and, indeed, most of us inside it are unaware of or unperturbed by the philosophical scandal of knowledge and go about our lives without too many epistemic anxieties. We hold our beliefs and presumptive knowledges more or less confidently, usually depending on how we acquired them (I saw it with my own eyes; I heard it on Fox News; a guy at the office told me) and how broadly and strenuously they seem to be shared or endorsed by various relevant people: experts and authorities, friends and family members, colleagues and associates. And we examine our convictions more or less closely, explain them more or less extensively, and defend them more or less vigorously, usually depending on what seems to be at stake for ourselves and/or other people and what resources are available for reassuring ourselves or making our beliefs credible to others (look, it's right here on the page; add up the figures yourself; I happen to be a heart specialist).

passage_3.text:
It's easy to forget that most of the world's languages are still transmitted orally with no widely established written form. While speech communities are increasingly involved in projects to protect their languages in print, on air and online - orality is fragile and contributes to linguistic vulnerability. But indigenous languages are about much more than unusual words and intriguing grammar: They function as vehicles for the transmission of cultural traditions, environmental understandings and knowledge about medicinal plants, all at risk when elders die and livelihoods are disrupted.

Both push and pull factors lead to the decline of languages. Through war, famine and natural disasters, whole communities can be destroyed, taking their language with them to the grave, such as the indigenous populations of Tasmania who were wiped out by colonists. More commonly, speakers live on but abandon their language in favor of another vernacular, a widespread process that linguists refer to as "language shift" from which few languages are immune. Such trading up and out of a speech form occurs for complex political, cultural and economic reasons sometimes voluntary for economic and educational reasons, although often amplified by state coercion or neglect. Welsh, long stigmatized and disparaged by the British state, has rebounded with vigor.

Many speakers of endangered, poorly documented languages have embraced new digital media with excitement. Speakers of previously exclusively oral tongues are turning to the web as a virtual space for languages to live on. Internet technology offers powerful ways for oral traditions and cultural practices to survive, even thrive, among increasingly mobile communities. I have watched as videos of traditional wedding ceremonies and songs are recorded on smartphones in London by Nepali migrants, then uploaded to YouTube and watched an hour later by relatives in remote Himalayan villages.

Globalization is regularly, and often uncritically, pilloried as a major threat to linguistic diversity. But in fact, globalization is as much process as it is ideology, certainly when it comes to language. The real forces behind cultural homogenization are unbending beliefs, exchanged through a globalized delivery system, reinforced by the historical monolingualism prevalent in much of the West.

Monolingualism, the condition of being able to speak only one language, is regularly accompanied by a deep-seated conviction in the value of that language over all others. Across the largest economies that make up the G8, being monolingual is still often the norm, with multilingualism appearing unusual and even somewhat exotic. The monolingual mindset stands in sharp contrast to the lived reality of most the world, which throughout its history has been more multilingual than unilingual. Monolingualism, then, not globalization, should be our primary concern.

Multilingualism can help us live in a more connected and more interdependent world. By widening access to technology, globalization can support indigenous and scholarly communities engaged in documenting and protecting our shared linguistic heritage. For the last 5,000 years, the rise and fall of languages was intimately tied to the plow, sword and book. In our digital age, the keyboard, screen and web will play a decisive role in shaping the future linguistic diversity of our species.

passage_4.text:
Many people believe that truth conveys power. Hence sticking with the truth is the best strategy for gaining power. Unfortunately, this is just a comforting myth. In fact, truth and power have a far more complicated relationship, because in human society, power means two very different things.

On the one hand, power mehaving the ability to manipulate objective realities: to hunt animals, to construct bridges, to cure diseases, to build atom bombs. This kind of power is closely tied to truth. If you believe a false physical theory, you won't be able to build an atom bomb. On the other hand, power also mehaving the ability to manipulate human beliefs, thereby getting lots of people to cooperate effectively. Building atom bombs requires not just a good understanding of physics, but also the coordinated labor of millions of humans. Planet Earth was conquered by Homo sapiens rather than by chimpanzees or elephants, because we are the only mammals that can cooperate in very large numbers. And large-scale cooperation depends on believing common stories. But these stories need not be true. You can unite millions of people by making them believe in completely fictional stories about God, about race or about economics. The dual nature of power and truth results in the curious fact that we humknow many more truths than any other animal, but we also believe in much more nonsense.

When it comes to uniting people around a common story, fiction actually enjoys three inherent advantages over the truth. First, whereas the truth is universal, fictions tend to be local. Consequently if we want to distinguish our tribe from foreigners, a fictional story will serve as a far better identity marker than a true story. The second huge advantage of fiction over truth has to do with the handicap principle, which says that reliable signals must be costly to the signaler. Otherwise, they can easily be faked by cheaters.... If political loyalty is signaled by believing a true story, anyone can fake it. But believing ridiculous and outlandish stories exacts greater cost, and is therefore a better signal of loyalty. Third, and most important, the truth is often painful and disturbing. Hence if you stick to unalloyed reality, few people will follow you. An American presidential candidate who tells the American public the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about American history has a 100100100 percent guarantee of losing the elections. An uncompromising adherence to the truth is an admirable spiritual practice, but it is not a winning political strategy.

Even if we need to pay some price for deactivating our rational faculties, the advantages of increased social cohesion are often so big that fictional stories routinely triumph over the truth in human history. Scholars have known this for thousands of years, which is why scholars often had to decide whether they served the truth or social harmony. Should they aim to unite people by making sure everyone believes in the same fiction, or should they let people know the truth even at the price of disunity?

questions.question_text: On the basis of the information in the passage, all of the following are true about the spiritual/material dichotomy of Indian nationalism EXCEPT that it:

options.label: A
options.text: helped in safeguarding the identity of Indian nationalism.

options.label: B
options.text: was not as ideologically powerful as the inner/outer dichotomy

options.label: C
options.text: represented a continuation of age-old oppositions in Indian culture

options.label: D
options.text: constituted the premise of the ghar/bāhir dichotomy

questions.explanation_text:
Step-by-step thought process:

The passage discusses how Indian nationalism used the spiritual/material split to deal with colonial challenges. Let's check what the passage actually says about each claim.

From passage: "The colonial situation, and the ideological response of nationalism to the critique of Indian tradition, introduced an entirely new substance to these dichotomies and effected their transformation."

The key word here is "introduced" and "transformation" -> This means the colonial period changed these ideas, not continued old ones.

Option Analysis:

🟢 Option 1 -> TRUE -> The passage clearly shows the spiritual/material split helped nationalism resist colonial dominance while keeping cultural identity safe.

🟢 Option 2 -> TRUE -> Passage directly states inner/outer dichotomy was "ideologically far more powerful" than material/spiritual distinction.

🔴 Option 3 -> FALSE -> Says these were "age-old oppositions" that just continued. But passage says colonial situation "introduced entirely new substance" and "effected their transformation" -> These weren't just old ideas continuing, they were transformed by colonialism.

🟢 Option 4 -> TRUE -> Material/spiritual dichotomy became inner/outer, which then became ghar/bāhir (home/world). Clear logical progression shown in passage.

From passage: "The colonial situation... introduced an entirely new substance to these dichotomies and effected their transformation."

Elimination logic: Options 1, 2, and 4 have direct textual support. Option 3 contradicts the passage's claim that colonialism transformed these ideas rather than just continuing ancient ones.

Answer: Option 3

questions.question_text: Which one of the following explains the "contradictory pulls" on Indian nationalism?

options.label: A
options.text: Despite its spiritual superiority, Indian nationalism had to fight against colonial domination.

options.label: B
options.text: Despite its scientific and technological inferiority, Indian nationalism had to fight against colonial domination.

options.label: C
options.text: Despite its fight against colonial domination, Indian nationalism had to borrow from the coloniser in the spiritual sphere.

options.label: D
options.text: Despite its fight against colonial domination, Indian nationalism had to borrow from the coloniser in the material sphere

questions.explanation_text:
The key to finding the "contradictory pulls" is to look for what created tension or conflict within Indian nationalist thinking.

From passage: "To overcome this domination, the colonized people had to learn those superior techniques of organizing material life and incorporate them within their own cultures. But this could not mean the imitation of the West in every aspect of life, for then the very distinction between the West and the East would vanish—the self-identity of national culture would itself be threatened."

The contradiction -> Indian nationalists wanted to fight Western domination BUT they also realized they needed to learn Western material techniques (science, technology) to become strong enough to fight that same domination. This created a pull in two opposite directions.

Think of it like this: You hate your enemy but you need to learn their fighting techniques to beat them. That's the contradiction!

Elimination Strategy: Look for the option that shows both sides of the tension - fighting against something while also needing something from that same source.

🔴 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Only mentions spiritual superiority and fighting, but misses the key contradictory pull about borrowing from the colonizer

🔴 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> Mentions inferiority and fighting, but again completely ignores the borrowing aspect that creates the real contradiction

🔴 Option 3 -> factual-error -> Says they borrowed in the spiritual sphere, which is completely wrong. The passage clearly says they preserved the spiritual and only borrowed material techniques

🟢 Option 4 -> captures the full contradiction -> Shows both sides perfectly: "despite fighting against" (resistance) + "had to borrow from" (dependence) + "in material sphere" (correct domain)

questions.question_text: Which one of the following, if true, would weaken the author's claims in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: The colonial period saw the hybridisation of Indian culture in all realms as it came in contact with British/European culture.

options.label: B
options.text: Forces of colonial modernity played an important role in shaping anti-colonial Indian nationalism.

options.label: C
options.text: The Industrial Revolution played a crucial role in shaping the economic prowess of Britain in the eighteenth century.

options.label: D
options.text: Indian nationalists rejected the cause of English education for women during the colonial period.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "But this could not mean the imitation of the West in every aspect of life, for then the very distinction between the West and the East would vanish—the self-identity of national culture would itself be threatened."

The author's main argument -> Indian nationalists created a smart separation: adopt Western material things (science, technology) but keep the spiritual core Indian and pure. This way they could get stronger without losing their identity.

The key claim -> Nationalists did NOT copy everything from the West. They were selective - took material stuff, kept spiritual stuff separate and protected.

Now we need to find which option attacks this main idea:

🟢 Option 1 -> directly contradicts -> says hybridization happened in ALL realms, but author says spiritual realm stayed separate and pure

🔴 Option 2 -> actually supports -> author agrees colonial forces shaped nationalism (that's his whole point!)

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> Industrial Revolution's role in British power doesn't touch author's claims about Indian nationalist ideology

🔴 Option 4 -> doesn't weaken -> rejecting English education for women could still fit within author's framework of protecting the "inner/home" sphere

The confusion students might have -> Option 4 seems like it could weaken because it shows rejection of Western influence. But remember, the author already says nationalists were selective, not totally accepting. Rejecting women's English education would actually support his claim about protecting the inner sphere.

Option 1 is the killer -> If culture got mixed up in every single area, then there was no separate spiritual sphere left untouched. This destroys the author's whole argument about selective adoption and protected inner identity.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following best describes the liberal perception of Indian nationalism?

options.label: A
options.text: Indian nationalist discourses provided an ideological principle of selection.

options.label: B
options.text: Indian nationalism's sophistication resided in its distinction of the material from the spiritual spheres.

options.label: C
options.text: Indian nationalist discourses reaffirmed traditional gender roles for Indian women.

options.label: D
options.text: Indian nationalism embraced the changes brought about by colonialism in Indian women's traditional gender roles.

questions.explanation_text:
Need to find the author's description of how liberals view Indian nationalism.

From passage: "It would be a grave error to see in this, as liberals are apt to in their despair at the many marks of social conservatism in nationalist practice, a total rejection of the West."

The key phrase -> "liberals are apt to in their despair at the many marks of social conservatism"

So liberals see nationalism as socially conservative, and this makes them upset. The passage shows nationalism kept women in traditional home roles while men handled the outside world.

🟠 Option 1 -> context-shift -> This describes what the AUTHOR argues (ideological selection principle), not what liberals think. Author uses this to defend nationalism against liberal criticism.

🟠 Option 2 -> context-shift -> Again, this is the AUTHOR'S analysis of nationalism's sophistication, not the liberal view. Liberals wouldn't call something they despair about "sophisticated."

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> Captures exactly what liberals see as "social conservatism" - keeping women in traditional gender roles (home/spiritual sphere). This matches their "despair" at conservative practices.

🟠 Option 4 -> opposite-meaning -> Says nationalism embraced changes in women's roles. But if it embraced changes, why would liberals despair about "social conservatism"? This contradicts the liberal perception of conservatism.

The confusion might be between options 1 and 3. Remember: Question asks for liberal perception, not the author's defense of nationalism. Option 1 is the author arguing back against liberals, while option 3 is what makes liberals upset in the first place.

questions.question_text: The author of the passage is most likely to support which one of the following statements?

options.label: A
options.text: The scandal of philosophy is that we might not know anything at all about reality if we think of reality as independent of our perceptions, ideas or descriptions.

options.label: B
options.text: The confidence with which we maintain something to be true is usually independent of the source of the alleged truth.

options.label: C
options.text: For the sceptic, if we think of reality as independent of our perceptions, ideas or descriptions, we should aim to know that reality independently too.

options.label: D
options.text: The actions taken on the basis of presumed knowledge are rational and justifiable if we are confident that that knowledge is widely held.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the author would support, not what any character in the passage supports. The author presents the philosophical problem clearly and explains different viewpoints.

Let us trace through the passage to understand the author's perspective on the "scandal of philosophy."

From passage: "The scandal is philosophy's apparent inability to show how, when and why we can be sure that we know something or, indeed, that we know anything."

From passage: "the sceptic's contention that we cannot be sure that we know anything at least not if we think of knowledge as something like having a correct mental representation of reality, and not if we think of reality as something like things as they are in themselves, independent of our perceptions, ideas or descriptions."

The author explains the problem: reality as "independent of our perceptions" -> we can't access it directly -> we can't compare our ideas to reality itself -> we can't be sure we know anything.

🔴 Option 2 -> directly contradicts passage -> The passage clearly states we hold beliefs "usually depending on how we acquired them" (source matters a lot!)

🔴 Option 3 -> misrepresents skeptic's position -> The skeptic says we CAN'T know reality independently, not that we SHOULD AIM TO

🔴 Option 4 -> unsupported claim -> Author presents the philosophical problem with presumed knowledge, doesn't endorse that wide confidence makes actions justifiable

🟢 Option 1 -> captures the core argument -> Author explains that if we think of reality as independent of our perceptions -> then the scandal emerges because we might not know anything at all about that reality

The key insight: The author presents the conditional logic perfectly - IF reality is independent of our perceptions THEN we face the scandal of potentially knowing nothing about it.

questions.question_text: "we cannot catch a glimpse of things-in-themselves around the corner of our own eyes; we cannot form an idea of reality that floats above the processes of our conceiving it " Which one of the following statements best reflects the argument being made in this sentence?

options.label: A
options.text: Our knowledge of reality cannot be merged with our process of conceiving it.

options.label: B
options.text: Our knowledge of reality floats above our subjective perception of it.

options.label: C
options.text: If the reality of things is independent of our perception, logically we cannot perceive that reality.

options.label: D
options.text: If the reality of things is independent of our eyesight, logically we cannot perceive our perception

questions.explanation_text:
We need to understand what the skeptic is arguing in that specific sentence. The sentence comes from the skeptic's argument about why we can't be sure we know anything. The skeptic is making a logical point about our limitations.

From passage: "since reality, under that conception of it, is outside our ken (we cannot catch a glimpse of things in themselves around the corner of our own eyes; we cannot form an idea of reality that floats above the processes of our conceiving it), we have no way to compare our mental representations with things as they are in themselves"

The skeptic's logic works like this: IF we define reality as something completely separate from our minds -> THEN we can never actually reach that reality -> THEREFORE we can't verify our knowledge claims.

The key insight: We're always trapped inside our own thinking processes. We can't step outside our minds to see reality "as it really is."

🔴 Option 1 -> context-shift -> talks about "merging" knowledge with conceiving, but the passage is about our inability to get outside our conceiving process to see independent reality

🔴 Option 2 -> opposite-meaning -> says our knowledge DOES float above perception, but the skeptic is arguing we CAN'T form ideas that float above our conceiving processes

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> captures the skeptic's conditional logic perfectly: IF reality is independent of perception, THEN we logically cannot perceive it (because we're always stuck inside our perceptual processes)

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> focuses on "eyesight" and "perceiving our perception" which misses the main point about accessing independent reality

The confusion students have: Options 1 and 3 both seem related to perception and reality. But Option 1 talks about "merging" (which isn't the issue), while Option 3 captures the core logical dilemma the skeptic presents.

questions.question_text: According to the last paragraph of the passage, “We hold our beliefs and presumptive knowledges more or less confidently, usually depending on” something. Which one of the following most broadly captures what we depend on?

options.label: A
options.text: All of the options listed here.

options.label: B
options.text: How much of a stake we have in them; what resources there are to support them

options.label: C
options.text: Remaining outside the academy; ignoring epistemic anxieties

options.label: D
options.text: How we come to hold them; how widely they are held in our social circles

questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace through the key sentence step by step.

From passage: "We hold our beliefs and presumptive knowledges more or less confidently, usually depending on how we acquired them (I saw it with my own eyes; I heard it on Fox News; a guy at the office told me) and how broadly and strenuously they seem to be shared or endorsed by various relevant people: experts and authorities, friends and family members, colleagues and associates."

The passage gives us two clear factors that determine our confidence:

  • How we got the belief (source) -> seeing it yourself vs hearing from someone else
  • How many relevant people agree (social support) -> experts, friends, family backing you up

🔴 Option 1 -> wrong assumption -> says "all options" are right, but let's check if that's true first

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> this talks about examining our beliefs (different part of paragraph), not what makes us confident in them

🔴 Option 3 -> completely irrelevant -> this is about ignoring the philosophical problem, not about confidence in beliefs

🟢 Option 4 -> perfect match -> "how we come to hold them" = how we acquired them, "how widely they are held in our social circles" = how broadly shared/endorsed by relevant people

Key insight: Don't get confused by other parts of the paragraph! The question asks specifically about what determines our confidence level, not about how we examine beliefs or handle philosophical problems.

Option 4 captures both factors mentioned in the passage perfectly.

questions.question_text: The author discusses all of the following arguments in the passage, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: sceptics believe that we can never fully know anything, if by "knowing" we mean knowledge of a reality that is independent of the knower.

options.label: B
options.text: if we cannot distinguish knowledge from opinion or delusion, we will not be able to justify our actions

options.label: C
options.text: philosophers maintain that the scandal of philosophy should be of concern to everyone

options.label: D
options.text: the best way to deal with scepticism about the veracity of knowledge is to ignore it

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "There are a number of ways to handle this situation. The most common is to ignore it."

The key insight here -> author describes what people actually do (ignore the problem) but never argues this is the best approach. Big difference between "most common" and "best way"!

Let's check what arguments ARE discussed:

• Sceptics say we can't know reality -> YES, discussed extensively in paragraph 2

• Can't distinguish knowledge from opinion = unjustified actions -> YES, paragraph 1

• Philosophers think everyone should care about this scandal -> YES, paragraph 1

But does author argue ignoring scepticism is the best way? -> NO! Author just observes it's what most people do.

🟢 Option 1 -> clearly discussed -> author explains sceptic's view about knowing independent reality

🟢 Option 2 -> clearly discussed -> author explains philosopher's argument about distinguishing knowledge from delusion

🟢 Option 3 -> clearly discussed -> author states philosophers believe this should concern everyone

🔴 Option 4 -> not argued as "best way" -> author only describes ignoring as "most common" behavior, never endorses it as the best approach

The passage describes ignoring as what people do, not what they should do. There's no argument that this is the best approach - just an observation about common behavior.

questions.question_text: The author mentions the Welsh language to show that:

options.label: A
options.text: while often pilloried, globalisation can, in fact, support linguistic revival.

options.label: B
options.text: efforts to integrate Welsh speakers in the English-speaking fold have been fruitless.

options.label: C
options.text: vulnerable languages can rebound with state effort.

options.label: D
options.text: languages can revive even after their speakers have gone through a “language shift”

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this,we need to understand why the author brings up Welsh as an example. Let us trace the context around the Welsh mention.

Step 1: Find where Welsh is mentioned and read the surrounding context

From passage: "More commonly, speakers live on but abandon their language in favor of another vernacular, a widespread process that linguists refer to as 'language shift' from which few languages are immune. Such trading up and out of a speech form occurs for complex political, cultural and economic reasons sometimes voluntary for economic and educational reasons, although often amplified by state coercion or neglect. Welsh, long stigmatized and disparaged by the British state, has rebounded with vigor."

Step 2: Understand the flow of ideas

Author discusses language decline -> explains "language shift" (people abandon their language) -> gives reasons (including state coercion/neglect) -> then gives Welsh as example

The key insight: Welsh was stigmatized and disparaged by the state (which causes language shift), but it "rebounded with vigor."

🟠 Option 1 -> context-shift -> Welsh example isn't about globalization at all. Author discusses globalization later in different paragraphs. Welsh example is specifically about language shift and state treatment.

🔴 Option 2 -> misses-the-point -> Says integration efforts were "fruitless" but passage shows Welsh actually succeeded in rebounding despite being disparaged. Gets the outcome completely wrong.

🔴 Option 3 -> opposite-meaning -> Says state effort helped, but passage clearly states Welsh was "stigmatized and disparaged by the British state" - state was working against it, not helping it. Welsh rebounded despite state opposition.

🟢 Option 4 -> captures the exact point -> Welsh speakers experienced language shift (due to state stigmatization), but the language still "rebounded with vigor" - proving languages can revive even after shift occurs.

The Welsh example perfectly illustrates that languages thought lost to "language shift" can still come back to life.

questions.question_text: From the passage, we can infer that the author is in favour of:

options.label: A
options.text: an expanded state role in the preservation of languages

options.label: B
options.text: cultural homogenisation

options.label: C
options.text: greater multilingualism

options.label: D
options.text: "language shifts" across languages

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what the author supports or favors based on their opinions in the passage. Let us trace through their main arguments.

The author discusses language loss, then shifts to what they think are the real problems and solutions. The key is in the later paragraphs where they reveal their position.

From passage: "Multilingualism can help us live in a more connected and more interdependent world" and "Monolingualism, then, not globalization, should be our primary concern."

The author's logic: Most people think globalization kills languages -> But actually, the real problem is monolingualism (speaking only one language) -> Multilingualism (speaking many languages) is the solution -> Technology can help support this.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> The passage mentions state actions (like British stigmatizing Welsh) but doesn't call for expanded state role. Author focuses on technology and individual multilingualism instead.

🔴 Option 2 -> opposite-stance -> Author directly criticizes cultural homogenization, calling it driven by "unbending beliefs." This goes against what author wants.

🔴 Option 4 -> negative-context -> "Language shift" means people abandoning their native languages for other ones. Author presents this as a problem causing language loss, not something good.

🟢 Option 3 -> direct-match -> Author explicitly states multilingualism helps us live in a "more connected world" and criticizes monolingualism as the main problem. This captures the author's clear position.

The confusion might be between options 1 and 3, but the author focuses on individual multilingualism and technology rather than government action.

questions.question_text: We can infer all of the following about indigenous languages from the passage EXCEPT that.

options.label: A
options.text: they are repositories of traditional knowledge about the environment and culture

options.label: B
options.text: people are increasingly working on documenting these languages.

options.label: C
options.text: their vocabulary and grammatical constructs have been challenging to document.

options.label: D
options.text: they are in danger of being wiped out as most can only be transmitted orally

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "But indigenous languages are about much more than unusual words and intriguing grammar: They function as vehicles for the transmission of cultural traditions, environmental understandings and knowledge about medicinal plants"

The passage talks about indigenous languages having unusual words and interesting grammar, but never says these are challenging to document -> in fact, it shows people are successfully documenting them through various projects.

Thought process: Read each option -> check if passage supports it -> find the one that's NOT supported

🟢 Option 1 -> supported -> passage clearly states they carry "cultural traditions, environmental understandings and knowledge about medicinal plants"

🟢 Option 2 -> supported -> passage says "speech communities are increasingly involved in projects to protect their languages in print, on air and online"

🔴 Option 3 -> not supported -> passage mentions "unusual words and intriguing grammar" but never says they are "challenging to document" - this assumption goes beyond what's written

🟢 Option 4 -> supported -> passage states "orality is fragile and contributes to linguistic vulnerability" and most languages are "transmitted orally with no widely established written form"

Student confusion: You might think Option 3 is correct because the passage mentions "unusual words and intriguing grammar" -> but unusual doesn't mean challenging to document. The passage actually shows people are successfully documenting these languages through digital media and other projects.

questions.question_text: The author lists all of the following as reasons for the decline or disappearance of a language EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: governments promoting certain languages over others

options.label: B
options.text: the focus on only a few languages as a result of widespread internet use

options.label: C
options.text: a catastrophic event that entirely eliminates a people and their culture.

options.label: D
options.text: people shifting away from their own language to study or work in another language

questions.explanation_text:
Need to find what's mentioned vs. what contradicts the passage.

From passage: "Speakers of previously exclusively oral tongues are turning to the web as a virtual space for languages to live on. Internet technology offers powerful ways for oral traditions and cultural practices to survive, even thrive"

From passage: "By widening access to technology, globalization can support indigenous and scholarly communities engaged in documenting and protecting our shared linguistic heritage"

Author clearly states internet helps preserve languages -> not causes decline. The question asks for what's not listed as a decline reason -> internet causing decline contradicts what author says.

Let's check what is mentioned as decline causes:

• War/disasters destroying communities -> "Through war, famine and natural disasters, whole communities can be destroyed, taking their language with them"

• Government policies -> "Welsh, long stigmatized and disparaged by the British state" and "state coercion or neglect"

• People switching languages -> "language shift" where speakers "abandon their language in favor of another vernacular" for "economic and educational reasons"

🟠 Option 1 -> mentioned in passage -> government "coercion" and "neglect" + Welsh example shows state policies harm languages

🟢 Option 2 -> contradicts passage -> author says internet helps preserve languages, not harm them - this is opposite of what passage states

🟠 Option 3 -> mentioned in passage -> "war, famine and natural disasters" destroying whole communities mentioned directly

🟠 Option 4 -> mentioned in passage -> "language shift" for "economic and educational reasons" described as common cause

questions.question_text: The author implies that, like scholars, successful leaders:

options.label: A
options.text: today know how to create social cohesion better than in the past.

options.label: B
options.text: know how to balance truth and social unity

options.label: C
options.text: use myths to attain the first type of power.

options.label: D
options.text: need to leverage both types of power to remain in office

questions.explanation_text:
First,we need to find what the passage says about scholars and their dilemma.

From passage: "Scholars have known this for thousands of years, which is why scholars often had to decide whether they served the truth or social harmony. Should they aim to unite people by making sure everyone believes in the same fiction, or should they let people know the truth even at the price of disunity?"

The passage shows scholars face a choice -> serve truth OR social harmony -> they must balance these two competing forces.

The author implies successful leaders face the same dilemma as scholars -> they must navigate between truth and social unity.

🔴 Option 1 -> unsupported comparison -> says leaders today are "better" than past leaders at social cohesion, but passage makes no past vs present comparison about leaders

🟢 Option 2 -> correct parallel -> captures the exact same dilemma scholars face - balancing truth vs social unity - which successful leaders must also navigate

🔴 Option 3 -> factual error -> says myths help with "first type of power" but passage clearly states first type of power (manipulating objective realities) needs truth, not myths. Myths help with second type of power (manipulating human beliefs)

🔴 Option 4 -> overstates with absolutes -> uses strong words "need" and "both" and "remain in office" - passage doesn't make such definitive claims about what leaders must do

The key insight -> successful leaders, like scholars, must choose how to balance serving truth versus maintaining social unity. Option 2 captures this balancing act perfectly.

questions.question_text: The central theme of the passage is about the choice between:

options.label: A
options.text: truth and power

options.label: B
options.text: stories that unite people and those that distinguish groups from each other

options.label: C
options.text: attaining social cohesion and propagating objective truth

options.label: D
options.text: leaders who unknowingly spread fictions and those who intentionally do so

questions.explanation_text:
The passage starts with truth vs power, but keep reading -> it narrows down to a specific choice scholars face. The final paragraph gives us the key.

From passage: "Scholars have known this for thousands of years, which is why scholars often had to decide whether they served the truth or social harmony. Should they aim to unite people by making sure everyone believes in the same fiction, or should they let people know the truth even at the price of disunity?"

Thought process: Passage discusses power -> shows two types of power -> explains how fiction beats truth for uniting people -> concludes with the scholar's dilemma between truth and social harmony/unity.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> truth and power are discussed, but the central theme is more specific - it's about choosing between truth and social cohesion, not just their relationship

🔴 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions one advantage of fiction (group identity) but misses the main choice between truth and unity that runs throughout

🟢 Option 3 -> captures both scope and nuance -> perfectly matches the core dilemma - scholars must choose between spreading objective truth or maintaining social cohesion through shared beliefs

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> passage never discusses the difference between leaders who knowingly vs unknowingly spread fiction - this distinction isn't made anywhere

The passage's central tension is: Do you tell people the truth (even if it divides them) or use fiction to keep society united?

questions.question_text: Regarding which one of the following quotes could we argue that the author over emphasises the importance of fiction?

options.label: A
options.text: scholars often had to decide whether they served the truth or social harmony. Should they aim to unite people by making sure everyone believes in the same fiction, or should they let people know the truth?

options.label: B
options.text: "Hence sticking with the truth is the best strategy for gaining power. Unfortunately, this is just a comforting myth."

options.label: C
options.text: "In fact, truth and power have a far more complicated relationship, because in human society, power me two very different things."

options.label: D
options.text: On the one hand, power me having the ability to manipulate objective realities: to hunt animals, to construct bridges, to cure diseases, to build atom bombs.*

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which quote shows the author giving too much importance to fiction.

The author argues that fiction has three big advantages over truth for uniting people, and that fictional stories often beat truth in human history because they create social unity.

From passage: "fictional stories routinely triumph over the truth in human history. Scholars have known this for thousands of years, which is why scholars often had to decide whether they served the truth or social harmony."

The key insight here -> the question asks about over-emphasis on fiction's importance. This meanswe need to find where the author might be giving fiction too much credit or making it seem more important than it really is.

Let us trace the thought process -> The author presents fiction as so powerful that even scholars must choose between truth and fiction for social unity. This could be seen as over-emphasizing fiction's role.

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> talks about truth being a "comforting myth" for gaining power, but doesn't mention fiction at all

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> explains that truth-power relationship is complicated, but again no mention of fiction

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> describes one type of power (manipulating reality), but completely ignores fiction

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> this quote presents fiction as so important that scholars must choose between serving truth OR using fiction for social harmony. This either/or framing could over-emphasize fiction's importance by suggesting it's the main way to achieve unity

The author presents this as a forced choice between truth and fiction, which might give fiction more importance than it deserves. The other three options don't even discuss fiction, so they can't be over-emphasizing its importance.

questions.question_text: The author would support none of the following statements about political power EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: people cannot handle the unvarnished truth, so leaders retain power by deviating from it.

options.label: B
options.text: while unalloyed truth is not recommended, leaders should stay as close as possible to it.

options.label: C
options.text: there are definite advantages to promoting fiction, but there needs to be some limit to a pervasive belief in myths.

options.label: D
options.text: manipulating people’s beliefs is politically advantageous, but a leader who propagates only myths is likely to lose power.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which statement the author would support about political power. The key is understanding the author's main argument about truth vs fiction in politics.

From passage: "the truth is often painful and disturbing. Hence if you stick to unalloyed reality, few people will follow you. An American presidential candidate who tells the American public the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth about American history has a 100 percent guarantee of losing the elections."

The author's core argument -> Truth doesn't win elections -> Fiction is better for gaining political power -> People prefer comforting lies over harsh realities.

Elimination process:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> "people cannot handle the unvarnished truth, so leaders retain power by deviating from it" -> This matches exactly what the author says. People find truth "painful and disturbing" so leaders who stick to truth lose followers.

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts passage -> "leaders should stay as close as possible to it [truth]" -> Author never recommends staying close to truth. In fact, he says fiction has advantages over truth and "uncompromising adherence to truth is not a winning political strategy."

🟠 Option 3 -> adds ideas not in passage -> talks about "limits" to believing myths -> Author never mentions any limits or boundaries. He actually says fictional stories "routinely triumph over truth."

🟠 Option 4 -> contradicts passage -> "a leader who propagates only myths is likely to lose power" -> Author suggests the opposite - that fiction gives political advantages and helps unite people effectively.

The author clearly supports the idea that people struggle with harsh truths, so successful leaders use fiction instead of reality to gain and keep power.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Look forward a few decades to an invention which can end the energy crisis, change the global economy and curb climate change at a stroke: commercial fusion power.
  2. To gain meaningful insights, logic has to be accompanied by asking probing questions of nature through controlled tests, precise observations and clever analysis.
  3. The greatest of all inventions is the uber-invention that has provided the insights on which others depend: the modern scientific method.
  4. This invention is inconceivable without the scientific method; it will rest on the application of a diverse range of scientific insights, such as the process transforming hydrogen into helium to release huge amounts of energy.
questions.explanation_text:
Let us trace the connections between ideas.

Step 1: Find the starting point -> Sentence 3 introduces a broad concept (scientific method as greatest invention)

Step 2: Look for explanations -> Sentence 2 explains how the scientific method works

Step 3: Find examples -> Sentence 1 gives a specific future invention (fusion power)

Step 4: Look for connections -> Sentence 4 links the example back to the main concept

From passage: "The greatest of all inventions is the uber-invention" (sentence 3) and "This invention is inconceivable without the scientific method" (sentence 4)

Thought Process:

Start broad -> explain details -> give example -> connect back

3 (introduces scientific method) -> 2 (explains how it works) -> 1 (gives fusion power example) -> 4 (connects fusion back to scientific method)

The word "this invention" in sentence 4 must refer to something mentioned just before -> that's "commercial fusion power" from sentence 1.

Since this question only has one correct answer and no wrong options to eliminate, the sequence is:

🟢 3214 -> Creates perfect logical flow from general concept to specific example and back to connection

The paragraph flows: Scientific method is greatest invention -> Here's how it works -> Here's a future example -> That example depends on scientific method

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

The unlikely alliance of the incumbent industrialist and the distressed unemployed worker is especially powerful amid the debris of corporate bankruptcies and layoffs. In an economic downturn, the capitalist is more likely to focus on costs of the competition emanating from free markets than on the opportunities they create. And the unemployed worker will find many others in a similar condition and with anxieties similar to his, which will make it easier for them to organize together. Using the cover and the political organization provided by the distressed, the capitalist captures the political agenda.

options.label: A
options.text: An unlikely alliance of the industrialist and the unemployed happens during an economic downturn in which they come together to unite politically and capture the political agenda.

options.label: B
options.text: In an economic downturn, the capitalists use the anxieties of the unemployed and their political organisation to set the political agenda to suit their economic interests.

options.label: C
options.text: The purpose of an unlikely alliance between the industrialist and the unemployed during an economic downturn is to stifle competition in free markets.

options.label: D
options.text: An economic downturn creates competition because of which the capitalists capture the political agenda created by the political organisation provided by the unemployed.

questions.explanation_text:
The key insight: Look for WHO does WHAT and HOW they do it. The passage shows capitalists using unemployed workers as a tool to get political power.

From passage: "Using the cover and the political organization provided by the distressed, the capitalist captures the political agenda."

This sentence is your answer key -> Capitalists USE unemployed workers' organization -> to capture political agenda for themselves.

How to eliminate wrong options:

Think like this: Who benefits? Who's using whom? The passage clearly shows capitalists are the ones benefiting by using unemployed workers.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> says both groups capture the agenda together, but passage shows only capitalist captures it using workers as cover

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures the manipulation perfectly: capitalists USE unemployed workers' fears and organization to set agenda for their OWN benefit

🔴 Option 3 -> irrelevant -> mentions "stifle competition" which isn't discussed anywhere in passage, goes off on tangent

🟠 Option 4 -> context-shift -> focuses on competition creating the agenda, but passage says capitalists capture agenda by USING unemployed workers' organization, not because of competition

Student confusion alert: You might think Option 1 sounds right because it mentions the alliance. But remember -> alliance doesn't mean equal partnership. The passage shows capitalists using workers, not working with them as equals.

The winner: Option 2 gets the power dynamic right -> capitalists exploit unemployed workers' situation for their own political gain.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. It has taken on a warm, fuzzy glow in the advertising world, where its potential is being widely discussed, and it is being claimed as the undeniable wave of the future.
  2. There is little enthusiasm for this in the scientific arena; for them marketing is not a science, and only a handful of studies have been published in scientific journals.
  3. The new, growing field of neuromarketing attempts to reveal the inner workings of consumer behaviour and is an extension of the study of how choices and decisions are made.
  4. Some see neuromarketing as an attempt to make the "art" of advertising into a science, being used by marketing experts to back up their proposals with some form of real data.
  5. The marketing gurus have already started drawing on psychology in developing tests and theories, and advertising people have borrowed the idea of the focus group from social scientists.
questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which four sentences work together and which one sentence doesn't fit the main topic.

From passage: "The new, growing field of neuromarketing attempts to reveal the inner workings of consumer behaviour"

This sentence introduces the main topic -> neuromarketing.

Step-by-step elimination process:

Sentences 1, 2, 3, 4 all focus on neuromarketing specifically:

  • Sentence 3 -> introduces neuromarketing as a field
  • Sentence 1 -> talks about "it" (neuromarketing) getting popular in advertising
  • Sentence 4 -> explains what people think about neuromarketing
  • Sentence 2 -> shows scientific community's view on neuromarketing

Sentence 5 -> talks about marketing in general borrowing from psychology and social scientists

The confusion students might have: "But sentence 5 mentions marketing too, so doesn't it fit?"

Key difference: Sentences 1-4 are all about the specific field of neuromarketing, while sentence 5 talks about general marketing practices borrowing from other fields.

Sentence 5 introduces social scientists and focus groups -> these concepts don't appear anywhere else in the other sentences.

🟢 Correct Answer: 5 -> scope-error -> talks about general marketing borrowing from various fields, while others focus specifically on neuromarketing as a distinct field

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Creativity is now viewed as the engine of economic progress. Various organizations are devoted to its study and promotion; there are encyclopedias and handbooks surveying creativity research. But this proliferating success has tended to erode creativity's stable identity: it has become so invested with value that it has become impossible to police its meaning and the practices that supposedly identify and encourage it. Many people and organizations committed to producing original thoughts now feel that undue obsession with the idea of creativity gets in the way of real creativity.

options.label: A
options.text: The industry that has built up around researching what comprises and encourages creativity has destroyed the creative process itself.

options.label: B
options.text: Creativity has proliferated to the extent that is no longer a stable process, and its mutating identity has stifled the creative process.

options.label: C
options.text: The value assigned to creativity today has assumed such proportions that the concept itself has lost its real meaning and this is hampering the engendering of real creativity.

options.label: D
options.text: The obsession with original thought, how it can be promoted and researched, has made it impossible for people and organizations to define the concept anymore.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what happens when something becomes too valued and how that affects the real thing itself.

From passage: "it has become so invested with value that it has become impossible to police its meaning and the practices that supposedly identify and encourage it"

From passage: "Many people and organizations committed to producing original thoughts now feel that undue obsession with the idea of creativity gets in the way of real creativity"

The passage shows a clear chain: Creativity gets valued highly -> Organizations study it everywhere -> This success makes creativity lose its clear meaning -> Too much focus on creativity actually blocks real creativity.

Think of it like this: When everyone talks about being "cool" all the time, trying to be cool actually makes you less cool. Same thing here with creativity.

Now let's see which option captures this idea best:

🔴 Option 1 -> degree-error -> Says the industry destroyed creativity, but passage says obsession just "gets in the way." Also blames the industry instead of the obsession itself.

🔴 Option 2 -> scope-error -> Says creativity itself proliferated, but passage says organizations studying creativity proliferated. Also wrongly suggests there was ever a "stable process" for creativity.

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> Captures the exact flow: high value -> lost meaning -> hampering real creativity. Matches both the cause (too much value) and effect (blocking real creativity).

🟠 Option 4 -> context-shift -> Focuses on defining creativity, but passage is about how obsession blocks creativity. Misses the main point about hampering real creative work.

Option 3 gets both parts right: the cause (too much value placed on creativity) and the effect (this actually hurts real creativity).

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

Biologists who publish their research directly to the Web have been labelled as "rogue", but physicists have been routinely publishing research digitally ("preprints"), prior to submitting in a peer-reviewed journal. Advocates of preprints argue that quick and open dissemination of research speeds up scientific progress and allows for wider access to knowledge. But some journals still don't accept research previously published as a preprint. Even if the idea of preprints is gaining ground, one of the biggest barriers for biologists is how they would be viewed by members of their conservative research community.

options.label: A
options.text: While digital publication of research is gaining popularity in many scientific disciplines, almost all peer-reviewed journals are reluctant to accept papers that have been published before.

options.label: B
options.text: Compared to biologists, physicists are less conservative in their acceptance of digital pre-publication of research papers, which allows for faster dissemination of knowledge.

options.label: C
options.text: One of the advantages of digital preprints of research is they hasten the dissemination process, but these are not accepted by most scientific communities.

options.label: D
options.text: Preprints of research are frowned on by some scientific fields as they do not undergo a rigourous reviewing process but are accepted among biologists as a quick way to disseminate information.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find the main contrast between how different scientific groups handle digital publishing.

From passage: "Biologists who publish their research directly to the Web have been labelled as 'rogue', but physicists have been routinely publishing research digitally"

The key insight -> passage shows a clear difference between two groups: biologists (seen as "rogue" for digital publishing) vs physicists (routinely do it). The passage also mentions benefits like faster progress and wider access.

Elimination process:

🔴 Option 1 -> degree-error -> says "almost all" journals reject preprints, but passage only says "some journals still don't accept." This overstates the problem - makes it sound worse than it really is.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> captures the main contrast perfectly. Physicists are "less conservative" than biologists (passage shows physicists do it routinely while biologists get labeled "rogue"). Also mentions faster dissemination benefit.

🟠 Option 3 -> scope-error -> says "most scientific communities" don't accept preprints, but passage shows physicists do accept them routinely. Also completely ignores the biologist vs physicist contrast, which is the main point of the passage.

🔴 Option 4 -> factually wrong -> says preprints are "accepted among biologists" but passage clearly states biologists who do this are labeled as "rogue" and face barriers from their "conservative research community." This gets it completely backwards.

The confusion might be between Options 2 and 3, but Option 3 misses the key comparison that drives the whole passage - the difference between how biologists and physicists handle digital publishing.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. The care with which philosophers examine arguments for and against forms of biotechnology makes this an excellent primer on formulating and assessing moral arguments.
  2. Although most people find at least some forms of genetic engineering disquieting, it is not easy to articulate why: what is wrong with re-engineering our nature?
  3. Breakthroughs in genetics present us with the promise that we will soon be able to prevent a host of debilitating diseases, and the predicament that our newfound genetic knowledge may enable us to enhance our genetic traits.
  4. To grapple with the ethics of enhancement, we need to confront questions that verge on theology, which is why modern philosophers and political theorists tend to shrink from them.
  5. One argument is that the drive for human perfection through genetics is objectionable as it represents a bid for mastery that fails to appreciate the gifts of human powers and achievements.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Look for the main topic → All sentences discuss genetics/genetic enhancement and philosophical arguments around it.

Step 2: Find which sentences connect naturally → Look for logical flow and consistent ideas.

From passage:

"Breakthroughs in genetics present us with the promise that we will soon be able to prevent a host of debilitating diseases, and the predicament that our newfound genetic knowledge may enable us to enhance our genetic traits."

"To grapple with the ethics of enhancement, we need to confront questions that verge on theology, which is why modern philosophers and political theorists tend to shrink from them."

Thought Process:

Sentence 3 introduces genetic enhancement → Sentence 2 explains why people find it troubling → Sentence 4 explains why philosophers avoid these hard questions → Sentence 5 gives one specific argument against enhancement.

These 4 sentences (2,3,4,5) flow together perfectly!

The Key Contradiction:

Sentence 4 says philosophers "shrink from" these questions

BUT

Sentence 1 says philosophers examine these arguments with "care"

This is a direct contradiction! One says they avoid, the other says they carefully study.

Since there are no options given in this question format, the answer is simply identifying which sentence number doesn't fit.

Answer: Sentence 1 is the odd one out because it contradicts the idea that philosophers avoid these difficult questions, instead claiming they examine them carefully.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. But today there is an epochal challenge to rethink and reconstitute the vision and practice of development as a shared responsibility a sharing which binds both the agent and the audience, the developed world and the developing, in a bond of shared destiny.
  2. We are at a crossroads now in our vision and practice of development.
  3. This calls for the cultivation of an appropriate ethical mode of being in our lives which enables us to realize this global and planetary situation of shared living and responsibility.
  4. Half a century ago, development began as a hope for a better human possibility, but in the last fifty years, this hope has lost itself in the dreary desert of various kinds of hegemonic applications.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the opening sentence

Sentence 2 says "We are at a crossroads now" -> This introduces the main topic without needing prior context. Perfect opener!

Step 2: What explains why we're at crossroads?

Sentence 4 gives historical background: "Half a century ago... but in the last fifty years" -> This explains why we're at crossroads by comparing past vs present.

Step 3: Look for connecting words

Sentence 1 starts with "But today" -> This directly contrasts with "Half a century ago" from sentence 4. Perfect connection!

Sentence 3 starts with "This calls for" -> The word "This" must refer to something specific mentioned before it.

From passage: "But today there is an epochal challenge to rethink and reconstitute the vision... This calls for the cultivation of an appropriate ethical mode"

Logical flow:

Crossroads (2) -> Why crossroads? Historical context (4) -> Today's challenge (1) -> What this challenge calls for (3)

Since this is a para jumble without multiple choice options, the process is about finding the natural sequence:

🟢 Correct sequence: 2413

  • Sentence 2 opens with the main idea
  • Sentence 4 provides historical background
  • Sentence 1 contrasts with "But today"
  • Sentence 3 follows with "This calls for" referring back to sentence 1's challenge

The flow is: Present situation -> Historical context -> Current challenge -> Solution needed

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. The US has long maintained that the Northwest Passage is an international strait through which its commercial and military vessels have the right to pass without seeking Canada's permission.
  2. Canada, which officially acquired the group of islands forming the Northwest Passage in 1880, claims sovereignty over all the shipping routes through the Passage.
  3. The dispute could be transitory, however, as scientists speculate that the entire Arctic Ocean will soon be ice-free in summer, so ship owners will not have to ask for permission to sail through any of the Northwest Passage routes.
  4. The US and Canada have never legally settled the question of access through the Passage, but have an agreement whereby the US needs to seek Canada's consent for any transit.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the opening sentence that introduces the topic

→ Sentence 2 introduces what Northwest Passage is (group of islands) and Canada's claim

→ This gives context before discussing the dispute

Step 2: Look for contrasting viewpoints

→ After Canada's claim (2), US position (1) naturally follows as contrast

→ "The US has long maintained..." shows opposing view

Step 3: Find current status of the issue

→ Sentence 4 talks about present agreement between both countries

→ This comes after establishing both positions

Step 4: Look for concluding/future statements

→ Sentence 3 starts with "The dispute could be..." referring back to established dispute

→ Talks about future resolution - perfect conclusion

From passage: "The dispute could be transitory, however..."

This "dispute" must refer back to something already mentioned → needs sentences 2, 1, 4 before it

Flow Logic: Introduction (what is it + Canada's claim) → US counter-position → Current agreement → Future outlook

Sequence: 2 → 1 → 4 → 3 = 2143

Check: Sentence 2 sets stage → 1 contrasts → 4 shows current status → 3 concludes with "the dispute" referring back to everything established above.
